also.hook: Alex Krizhevsky was a graduate student in computer science at the University of Toronto, working under Geoffrey Hinton alongside fellow student Ilya Sutskever. In 2012 the three published ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, describing a large convolutional network, later known as AlexNet, that used GPU training and a new regularization technique to sharply cut image classification error rates. A variant of the network won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that year by a wide margin, a result widely credited with convincing the broader field that deep neural networks, trained at scale on GPUs, could outperform earlier computer vision approaches. Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton founded DNNresearch Inc. to build on the work, and in March 2013 Google acquired the company, bringing Krizhevsky and Sutskever onto Google's research staff while Hinton divided his time between Google and the university.
also.name: Alex Krizhevsky

also.hook: David Rumelhart earned a bachelors degree in psychology and mathematics from the University of South Dakota before completing a PhD in mathematical psychology at Stanford University in 1967. He then joined the faculty at the University of California, San Diego, where he helped build the Parallel Distributed Processing research group that modeled cognition as patterns of activity distributed across networks of simple units. With Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, he co-authored the 1986 Nature paper Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors, which showed how multilayer neural networks could be trained efficiently and became one of the founding texts of modern deep learning. That same year he and James McClelland published the two volume Parallel Distributed Processing, Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, which brought connectionist ideas to a wide audience of psychologists, neuroscientists and computer scientists. He returned to Stanford as a professor in 1987, continuing his work in cognitive science until a neurodegenerative illness ended his research career in the late 1990s. He died in Chelsea, Michigan, on March 13, 2011, at the age of 68.
also.name: David Rumelhart

also.hook: Hinton kept faith with neural networks through two AI winters, and won. The training method he championed in 1986 and the 2012 breakthrough his lab produced turned a marginal idea into the technology behind modern AI. Then, at the peak of vindication, he quit Google to warn the world about what he had helped build, giving AI risk its most credentialed voice.
also.name: Geoffrey Hinton

also.hook: Leo Breiman earned a physics degree from Caltech in 1949, a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia in 1950, and a PhD from UC Berkeley in 1954, after which he taught probability theory at UCLA. He later resigned his tenured position to spend more than a decade as an independent statistical consultant, working on problems like traffic pattern and ozone level prediction, before joining the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980. With Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees, published in 1984, and in 1996 he introduced Bagging, a method of averaging predictions across bootstrap samples to reduce variance. In 2001 he introduced Random Forests, an ensemble of randomized decision trees that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms, and published Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, an influential essay on competing approaches to statistical inference. He died at his home in Berkeley, California, on July 5, 2005, following a prolonged illness.
also.name: Leo Breiman
also.moniker: Professor of Statistics, University of California, Berkeley

also.hook: Vladimir Vapnik developed much of the mathematical foundation that modern machine learning still relies on. Born in Tashkent in the Soviet Union, he earned his doctorate in statistics from the Institute of Control Sciences in Moscow in 1964, where he later headed the computer science research department. Working with Alexey Chervonenkis, he developed what became known as Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory, a mathematical framework for understanding when and why a learning algorithm can generalize from training data to new examples. After moving to the United States, he joined AT&T Bell Labs, where he and colleagues including Corinna Cortes, Bernard Boser, and Isabelle Guyon turned his theoretical work into the support vector machine, a classification method described in a landmark 1995 paper with Cortes and in a US patent he shares with Boser and Guyon. He went on to hold research and teaching positions at NEC Laboratories, Royal Holloway University of London, Columbia University, and Facebook AI Research, continuing to develop and extend statistical learning theory.
also.name: Vladimir Vapnik
also.moniker: Co-inventor of the support vector machine and statistical learning theory

profiles.hook: A century before electronic computers existed, Lovelace saw what they would become. Her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine contain the first published algorithm written for a machine, and, more radically, the first argument that such machines could work on any symbol, not just numbers. Every general-purpose computer vindicates that insight.

profiles.hook: Allen Newell trained as a physicist at Stanford before shifting into mathematics and, after a year at Princeton, joining the RAND Corporation in 1950 to study Air Force logistics and organizational decision making. At RAND he began a long collaboration with Herbert Simon, and in 1955 and 1956 the two of them, working with programmer J.C. Shaw, built the Logic Theorist, a program that could prove theorems from Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica by searching through possible proof steps rather than brute calculation. Newell earned his doctorate at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, where his dissertation grew out of that work, and he joined the Carnegie faculty in 1961, remaining there for the rest of his career. With Simon he went on to build the General Problem Solver, a program meant to capture general human problem solving through means-ends analysis, and the two argued that computers manipulating symbols could serve as a general theory of intelligence, a position they called the physical symbol system hypothesis. In his final years Newell developed Soar, a unified cognitive architecture meant to explain the full range of human cognitive behavior within a single computational framework, and he laid out that ambition in his 1990 book Unified Theories of Cognition. He died of cancer in 1992, shortly after the field had already recognized the sweep of his work through its highest honors.

profiles.hook: Arthur Samuel trained as an electrical engineer at MIT before spending nearly two decades at Bell Telephone Laboratories working on vacuum tubes and related electronics. After a period teaching at the University of Illinois, he joined IBM in 1949, where he worked on the design of the IBM 701 and 704 computers. In his own time at IBM he wrote a program that played checkers, and rather than encoding a fixed strategy he had it improve through repeated self-play, adjusting its evaluation of board positions based on outcomes and building a memory of positions it had already assessed. He described the work in a 1959 paper in the IBM Journal of Research and Development, using the phrase machine learning to describe a computer's ability to improve at a task without being explicitly reprogrammed for it. Samuel demonstrated an early version of the program on television in 1956, and it stood for years as a widely cited proof that a machine could improve through experience. He moved to Stanford University in 1966, where he continued refining the checkers program and working on computing research until his death in 1990.

profiles.hook: Claude Shannon studied electrical engineering and mathematics at the University of Michigan before arriving at MIT, where his 1937 master's thesis showed that Boolean algebra could be used to design and simplify electrical switching circuits, groundwork that digital computer design would later depend on. He earned a PhD in mathematics from MIT in 1940 and spent the years after at Bell Telephone Laboratories, where during the Second World War he worked on fire-control systems and cryptography, producing a classified analysis of secrecy systems that he published openly after the war. In 1948 he published A Mathematical Theory of Communication in the Bell System Technical Journal, defining information mathematically in terms of entropy and showing how much data could reliably be sent over a noisy channel, work that founded information theory and underlies how modern computing represents and transmits information. He returned to MIT as a professor in 1956, continuing his research in communication theory while also experimenting with early electromechanical devices, including a maze-solving device called Theseus that used simple relays to learn a path, an early demonstration of machine memory and adaptive behavior. His concepts of the bit, entropy and channel capacity gave computing a rigorous vocabulary for measuring and manipulating information, an influence that reaches into how artificial intelligence systems handle information and uncertainty. He died in 2001 after some years of declining health.

profiles.hook: Donald Hebb trained first in English literature at Dalhousie University before turning to psychology, earning a master's degree at McGill University and then a PhD at Harvard under Karl Lashley, whose research on the brain's role in learning shaped Hebb's own direction. After periods at Queen's University and the Yerkes Laboratories of Primate Biology, he joined McGill University in 1947, where he spent the rest of his career and eventually chaired the psychology department. In 1949 he published The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory, proposing that learning and memory arise physically in the brain when one neuron's repeated activity helps fire another, strengthening the connection between them, a mechanism now known as Hebbian learning or Hebb's postulate. That idea gave later researchers a concrete, biologically grounded rule for how neural connections might change with experience, and it became a founding principle for artificial neural network models, from Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron through much later connectionist research. Hebb also developed the Hebb-Williams maze for testing animal intelligence and studied how early experience and sensory deprivation shape later behavior. He remained closely tied to McGill until his death in 1985, having also served as the university's chancellor.

profiles.hook: Edward Feigenbaum studied electrical engineering at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, where he also earned his PhD under Herbert Simon, building EPAM, an early computer model of human memory and learning. He joined the faculty at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1960 and moved to Stanford University in 1965, where he spent most of his career and later chaired the computer science department. At Stanford he worked with the geneticist Joshua Lederberg on DENDRAL, a program that inferred the molecular structure of chemical compounds from mass spectrometry data by encoding the reasoning of expert chemists, widely regarded as the first true expert system. Feigenbaum and his colleagues went on to build MYCIN, a program that used a similar rule-based approach to help diagnose bacterial infections and recommend antibiotic treatment, and his work established knowledge engineering, the practice of capturing human expertise as computable rules, as a distinct discipline within artificial intelligence. He directed Stanford's Knowledge Systems Laboratory for many years, served as chief scientist of the United States Air Force from 1994 to 1997, and in 1994 shared the A.M. Turing Award with Raj Reddy for demonstrating the practical and commercial potential of large-scale artificial intelligence systems.

profiles.hook: Frank Rosenblatt studied psychology at Cornell University, earning his PhD there in 1956, and went to work at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in Buffalo, New York, where he began developing a mathematical model of how the brain might learn to recognize patterns. In 1957 and 1958 he built the Perceptron, a network of simple, adjustable units loosely modeled on neurons, and described it in a 1958 paper as a probabilistic model for information storage and pattern recognition in the brain. With funding from the Office of Naval Research, he and his collaborators built a physical version called the Mark I Perceptron, using potentiometers to represent adjustable connection weights and motors to carry out the learning process, and it could learn to distinguish simple visual patterns after being shown examples. The 1958 unveiling drew wide press coverage and considerable hype about the machine's potential, though the model's practical limitations, later highlighted in Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons, contributed to a broader cooling of interest in neural network research for years afterward. Rosenblatt later became a professor at Cornell University in Ithaca, working in brain and behavioral sciences and continuing to study perceptron-like models until his death in a boating accident on Chesapeake Bay in 1971. Decades later the layered, adjustable-weight structure he pioneered became the basis for the neural networks used throughout modern artificial intelligence, and the Smithsonian now holds the original Mark I Perceptron in its collection.

profiles.hook: Herbert Simon entered the University of Chicago in 1933 hoping to become what he called a mathematical social scientist, studying under mentors including the logician Rudolf Carnap and political scientist Charles Merriam. After finishing his undergraduate degree in 1936 and later a PhD, he built a career studying how organizations and individuals actually make decisions under limits of time, knowledge and computing power, a theory he called bounded rationality. In 1949 he joined the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University, to help build its Graduate School of Industrial Administration around economics and behavioral science. Around 1954 he began working with Allen Newell to use computer simulation to study human problem solving, and together with Cliff Shaw they built the Logic Theorist in 1956, widely considered the first program designed to mimic human reasoning, followed by the more general General Problem Solver in 1957. Simon spent the rest of his career at Carnegie Mellon studying cognition, organizations and artificial intelligence, work recognized with the 1975 ACM Turing Award, shared with Newell, and the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research on decision making in economic organizations.

profiles.hook: J.C.R. Licklider trained as an experimental psychologist, earning his PhD at the University of Rochester before working on psychoacoustics at Harvard during the Second World War. He later moved into engineering circles at MIT, where hands-on exposure to early computers convinced him that machines could become active partners in human thought rather than passive calculators. In 1957 he ran a self study tracking his own workday and found that most of his time went to mechanical tasks that stood between him and actual thinking, an observation that fed directly into his influential 1960 paper Man-Computer Symbiosis, which argued that people and computers should work together in close, real time partnership. In 1962 he became the first director of the Information Processing Techniques Office at the Advanced Research Projects Agency, where he funded university computer science research across the country and, in an internal 1963 memo, sketched an early vision of computers linked together into what he called an intergalactic network. That funding program and the community of researchers it supported helped lay the intellectual groundwork that led to the ARPANET later in the decade.

profiles.hook: John McCarthy earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Caltech in 1948 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1951. In August 1955, together with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon, he wrote the proposal for a summer research project at Dartmouth College built on the idea that every aspect of learning or intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it, a document that introduced the field's name. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop that followed brought together many of the researchers who would go on to define artificial intelligence as a discipline. While at MIT in 1958, McCarthy created the Lisp programming language, which became the dominant tool for AI research for decades because of its ability to manipulate symbolic expressions. He moved to Stanford University in 1962, where he founded the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and continued developing logic based approaches to reasoning and knowledge representation until his retirement in 2000.

profiles.hook: Judea Pearl earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the Technion in Israel in 1960, then went on to complete master's degrees in electronics and physics in the United States before earning a PhD in electrical engineering from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn in 1965. He joined the computer science faculty at UCLA in 1969 and later founded its Cognitive Systems Laboratory. In the 1980s Pearl developed Bayesian networks, a mathematical framework for representing and reasoning about uncertain relationships among many variables, set out in his 1988 monograph Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems, which reshaped how artificial intelligence systems handle uncertainty. He then turned to an even harder problem, building a formal calculus, including what he called the do-calculus, for distinguishing genuine causation from mere correlation using data, work collected in his 2000 book Causality. He later explained these ideas for a general audience in The Book of Why, published in 2018. For this body of work he received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 2011.

profiles.hook: Lotfi Zadeh was born in Baku and later studied in Tehran before completing further degrees at MIT and Columbia University. He spent nine years on the electrical engineering faculty at Columbia before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1959, where he later chaired the Electrical Engineering Department from 1963 to 1968 and helped rename it the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences. In 1965 he published the paper Fuzzy Sets in the journal Information and Control, introducing a mathematical framework for representing categories that admit degrees of membership rather than strict true or false boundaries. That single paper launched fuzzy set theory and, later, fuzzy logic, which spread from control engineering into consumer electronics, decision analysis and approaches to reasoning under uncertainty in artificial intelligence. Zadeh remained a prolific researcher at Berkeley for the rest of his career, publishing more than two hundred papers and receiving numerous honors including the IEEE Medal of Honor and the Benjamin Franklin Medal.

profiles.hook: Marvin Minsky earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Harvard in 1950 and a PhD in mathematics from Princeton in 1954, having already built SNARC, an early neural network learning machine, as a student in 1951. In 1955 he joined John McCarthy, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon in writing the proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, and in 1959 he co-founded what became the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with McCarthy, directing it for many years. In 1969, with Seymour Papert, Minsky published Perceptrons, a rigorous mathematical analysis of the capabilities and limits of a simple class of neural networks that influenced the direction of AI research for years afterward. He later developed frame theory as a way of representing knowledge in AI systems, and in 1985 published Society of Mind, arguing that intelligence emerges from the interaction of many simple, specialized processes rather than any single mechanism. Minsky received the ACM A.M. Turing Award in 1969 for his central role in creating, shaping and advancing the field of artificial intelligence.

profiles.hook: Nils Nilsson earned his PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford in 1958, then served in the United States Air Force before joining SRI International, where he spent 23 years building foundational tools for artificial intelligence. At SRI he co-invented the A* search algorithm and the STRIPS automated planning system, and co-directed Shakey, one of the first mobile robots able to perceive its surroundings, plan, and act. He returned to Stanford in 1985 and chaired its Computer Science Department until 1990, later becoming the Kumagai Professor of Engineering, Emeritus. Nilsson wrote nine books on artificial intelligence, including the 2010 history The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, and served as president of AAAI. He died in 2019 in Medford, Oregon, at age 86.

profiles.hook: Norbert Wiener was a mathematical prodigy who earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts College at 14 and a PhD in philosophy from Harvard at 19, then studied with Bertrand Russell in Cambridge and David Hilbert in Gottingen. He joined MIT's Department of Mathematics in 1919 and remained there for 45 years, doing foundational work in stochastic processes, harmonic analysis, and what became known as the Wiener process. During the Second World War he worked on statistical prediction methods for anti-aircraft fire control, research that pushed him toward a broader theory of control and communication. In 1948 he published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics and giving later computing and AI research a vocabulary for feedback loops. His 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings extended these ideas to society, warning early about the social effects of automation. He became an MIT Institute Professor in 1959 and died in 1964 while traveling in Stockholm, Sweden.

profiles.hook: Paul Werbos studied economics at the London School of Economics before earning a PhD from Harvard University in 1974, where his dissertation, Beyond Regression, described how the chain rule for ordered derivatives could train neural network-like models, work later recognized as the first description of backpropagation. Through the 1980s he worked as an econometric forecasting analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration, applying related statistical modeling techniques. In 1988 he joined the National Science Foundation as a program director, where he spent over two decades directing funding for research on adaptive systems and neural networks before retiring in 2015. His dissertation was later republished as the book The Roots of Backpropagation (Wiley, 1994), and he went on to develop related ideas under the name adaptive dynamic programming, connecting neural networks with dynamic programming based control. In 2011 the International Neural Network Society gave him its Hebb Award, its highest honor.

quick_facts: Described the chain rule for ordered derivatives, the mathematical basis of backpropagation, in his 1974 Harvard PhD dissertation.
His dissertation was republished as the book The Roots of Backpropagation (Wiley, 1994).
Also developed adaptive dynamic programming, linking neural networks with dynamic programming based control methods.
Worked as an econometric forecasting analyst at the U.S. Energy Information Administration from 1980 to 1989.
Served as a National Science Foundation program director from 1988 until his retirement in 2015.
Received the International Neural Network Society's Hebb Award in 2011 and is a Fellow of IEEE.

profiles.hook: Raj Reddy earned a bachelor's degree in engineering from Guindy Engineering College at the University of Madras in 1958, a master's from the University of New South Wales in 1960, and a PhD in computer science from Stanford University in 1966. He joined Carnegie Mellon University as an associate professor in 1969 and led development of the Hearsay speech understanding systems, early efforts to combine multiple knowledge sources for recognizing connected speech. In 1979 he became the founding director of Carnegie Mellon's Robotics Institute, building it into one of the world's leading robotics research centers, and later served as dean of the School of Computer Science from 1991 to 1999. In 1994 he shared the ACM Turing Award with Edward Feigenbaum for pioneering the design of large-scale artificial intelligence systems. He has also worked on extending computing access to underserved populations, including projects aimed at low-cost computing and digital libraries for developing regions.

profiles.hook: Seymour Papert earned a PhD in mathematics from the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa in 1952 and a second PhD from Cambridge University in 1958, then studied children's cognitive development with Jean Piaget at the University of Geneva. He joined MIT in 1963, became a professor of applied mathematics in 1967, and co-directed MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with Marvin Minsky, with whom he co-authored the 1969 book Perceptrons, an influential mathematical analysis of early neural networks. Drawing on his work with Piaget, Papert co-developed the Logo programming language and its turtle graphics for children, and in his 1980 book Mindstorms: Children, Computers, and Powerful Ideas he set out constructionism, an educational theory holding that children learn best by building and creating things themselves. He became a founding faculty member of the MIT Media Lab in 1985 and in 2004 co-founded the One Laptop per Child initiative to extend computing access to children in developing countries. After suffering a serious brain injury in a 2006 accident in Hanoi, Vietnam, he died in 2016 at his home in Maine.

quick_facts: Co-developed the Logo programming language and its turtle graphics, the first programming environment designed for children.
Founded constructionism, an educational philosophy holding that children learn best by actively building and creating things.
Co-authored Perceptrons (1969) with Marvin Minsky, an influential mathematical study of early neural network limitations.
Co-directed MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with Marvin Minsky before becoming a founding faculty member of the MIT Media Lab in 1985.
Co-founded the One Laptop per Child initiative in 2004 to bring low-cost computers to children worldwide.
Studied children's cognitive development under Jean Piaget in Geneva before bringing those ideas into computing and education.
